faqs.q: How do I check if my village is at risk?
faqs.a: Open 'Check my area' from the menu. Type your village or town name and press Search, or press 'Use my location'. You will see a colour, a word (High, Moderate or Low) and what to do.

faqs.q: What do High, Moderate and Low mean?
faqs.a: They compare your place with other places in the same state. High means landslides are more likely there than in most places. Low means less likely, but still possible in heavy rain. It is not a promise that a landslide will or will not happen.

faqs.q: The result says HIGH RISK. What should I do?
faqs.a: Do not panic. In heavy rain stay away from steep slopes and roads below cliffs. Watch for cracks in the ground, leaning trees or poles, and muddy stream water. If you see any, move away and tell your local authority. Keep a torch, a charged phone and important papers ready.

faqs.q: What is a rain alert?
faqs.a: Many days of rain can make a slope give way. A rain alert means the rain in an area has reached a level that research has linked to landslides there. It is a warning to be careful, not proof that a landslide has happened.

faqs.q: Why does it say 'not assessed' or 'rain alerts are not switched on'?
faqs.a: Our map covers road stretches in the north-east states where we have data. If your place is far from any road we have assessed, we say so instead of guessing. Rain alerts are switched on for Sikkim only for now. Other states still show risk levels and rainfall, but no alerts yet.

faqs.q: Who do I call in an emergency?
faqs.a: Call 112 (national emergency) or 1077 (disaster helpline). The Emergency Contacts page in the menu has more helpline numbers. Numbers marked 'Unconfirmed' should be checked before you rely on them.

faqs.q: How do I report a crack or a landslide?
faqs.a: Use the citizen reporting app: send a photo, your place and a short note. An officer will check it. If someone is in danger, call 112 first.

faqs.q: How do I change the language?
faqs.a: Use the globe button at the top of the screen and choose English, हिन्दी or नेपाली. Your choice is remembered on that device.

faqs.q: Can I listen to the answer instead of reading it?
faqs.a: On the 'Check my area' result there is a 'Listen' button that reads the result aloud. It appears only if your phone or computer has a voice for the language you chose. If you do not see it, ask someone to read it to you, or call the helpline.

faqs.q: Is the rainfall shown live?
faqs.a: It comes from a weather service (Open-Meteo) and is refreshed about every hour. Today and past days are the service's estimate. The next two days are a forecast and are marked that way.

faqs.q: Does this predict when a landslide will happen?
faqs.a: No. It shows which places are more prone to landslides because of the land itself, and it warns when rain reaches a dangerous level. It cannot say when or where a particular landslide will happen. Always follow warnings from your local authority.

faqs.q: What if the road near me is blocked by a landslide?
faqs.a: An alert means dangerous rain, not that the road is blocked. If you see a slide or a blockage, stay away from it, call 112 or 1077, and report it in the citizen reporting app so an officer can check it. On a road stretch's page you can see the villages and the nearest hospital, police and fire station around it (from OpenStreetMap, straight-line distances). This system does not know which villages would be cut off, where evacuation centres are, or how long rescue would take — ask your district control room (1077) about shelters and rescue.

faqs.q: What am I supposed to check first thing in the morning?
faqs.a: Open the Overview page. Read the cards at the top, then the map, then the Active Alerts panel. 'High Risk Zones' counts the highest-scoring zones in each state. Risk levels are relative to other zones in the same state, so use it to decide where to look first, not to compare one state with another. Beside the rainfall chart, check 'Rainfall updated … ago' to see how fresh the data is.

faqs.q: How do I find one particular village, alert or incident quickly?
faqs.a: Use the search box at the top of any page, or press Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on a Mac), to find zones, alerts and reports by name. To assess a village or town by its ordinary name, use 'Check my area' instead — road stretches have codes like NH10, not village names.

faqs.q: How often does the information on screen change?
faqs.a: Rainfall is refreshed about every hour, and opening the Overview refreshes it if it is over two and a half hours old. New alerts appear on screen as soon as they are raised. Other pages load fresh each time you open them.

faqs.q: What does the state selector at the top do?
faqs.a: It filters the pages by state. Choose a state and the Overview, Alerts, Highway Corridors, Authority Contacts, Emergency Contacts, Incidents and Citizen Reports show only that state; 'All States' shows everything. Authority Contacts always also shows contacts registered for all states, and a Critical broadcast calls the officials of the alert's own state plus those. If a state has no alerts, contacts or records, the page says so — for a state where rain alerts are switched off (everything except Sikkim today) it says that, so an empty list is not read as safety. Pages that are the same everywhere (Help, Data Sources & Methodology) do not change.

faqs.q: Can I use this on a phone or tablet?
faqs.a: Yes on a tablet — the layout adjusts. On a small phone the side menu is hidden behind a button and the dashboard is cramped; it is meant for a desk or control-room display. Residents on phones can use 'Check my area', which is built for small screens.

faqs.q: Where do I find public helpline numbers to give someone?
faqs.a: The Emergency Contacts page in the side menu — a click-to-call directory of public helplines. Numbers already confirmed real can be called directly; anything not yet independently confirmed is clearly marked 'Unconfirmed — verify before real-world use'.

faqs.q: What do the coloured circles on the map mean?
faqs.a: Each circle is a road stretch that has been assessed. Its colour is its risk level: terracotta (red-brown) for High, turmeric (yellow-orange) for Moderate, green for Low. Zoomed out, nearby stretches are grouped into one circle showing how many there are. Risk levels are relative: each colour ranks a stretch against other stretches in the same state (High is roughly the top third), so a High stretch in one state is not necessarily as dangerous as a High stretch in another.

faqs.q: What is 'susceptibility', and how is it different from risk?
faqs.a: Susceptibility is a score from 0 to 100% from a computer model that looks at the land itself — such as slope and ground cover — compared with where landslides have happened before. The risk level (High, Moderate, Low) is that score split into three bands. Neither changes with today's weather. Rain works separately, through alerts.

faqs.q: Why did a zone change colour? / Why is a zone High with no alert?
faqs.a: Colours only change when the model is re-run with new data, not when it rains. Rain works through alerts: when rainfall reaches the danger level for a zone, an alert is raised. So a zone can be High on the map with no alert on a dry day, and a Low zone can still get an alert after a lot of rain.

faqs.q: What does the dashed line on the rainfall chart mean?
faqs.a: It is the daily rainfall danger level for that zone. It comes from published research on rain and landslides for the region, and is lowered for zones with higher risk. It is drawn only for states where rain alerts are switched on (Sikkim today). For Sikkim the research source has not yet been checked against the paper's full text, so treat the level as a working value.

faqs.q: A village I know is at risk is not shown on the map. Why?
faqs.a: The map shows road stretches, not every village. Zones are built from the main roads in each state, because that is where the landslide records are. To see the risk near a village, use 'Check my area' — it shows the nearest assessed road, and says clearly if none is near.

faqs.q: I clicked a circle on the map and it opened a new page. What is that?
faqs.a: That is Zone Detail — the zone's own page with its score, the model version that scored it, its rainfall chart and every alert raised for it. For zones we do not keep rainfall for, the chart is fetched live and marked 'not stored'. Use Back to return.

faqs.q: What does the Highway Corridors page show that the map doesn't?
faqs.a: The same zones grouped by highway or road code (for example NH310A) instead of listed one by one — so you can see which whole corridor has the worst risk, how many active alerts sit on it, and its highest-risk stretch. Useful for a corridor-level decision such as a road closure.

faqs.q: An alert has just appeared. What am I expected to do?
faqs.a: Read the location and severity, check that zone on the map, then follow your district's standard operating procedure for that severity. This dashboard tells you what the system has detected; the decision to evacuate or close a road is yours.

faqs.q: Does the public get warned automatically?
faqs.a: Partly. When a rain alert is raised in Sikkim, the system sends an SMS to subscribed citizen numbers automatically. It is a real SMS service (Twilio), but on a trial account it can only reach numbers verified in advance, so it is not yet a state-wide public warning system. Your job on the ground stays the same.

faqs.q: Who exactly receives those SMS messages?
faqs.a: People who have submitted a citizen report (their phone number is kept for this), plus the officials on the Authority Contacts page for Critical broadcasts. There is no public sign-up yet, so a village not receiving warnings has simply not been added.

faqs.q: Where does the scrolling text at the top of the screen come from?
faqs.a: It shows the newest real active rain alerts from the system (the latest few, then a count of the rest). It is not a weather-service bulletin. Each alert's sentence is written in English when the alert is raised. If nothing is active it says so, and names the states where alerts are switched on. Hover over the strip to stop it scrolling.

faqs.q: An alert is showing but the weather here is fine. Is it wrong?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Check the 'Rain now' line on the alert and the zone's rainfall chart. Alerts are based on rain over the last several days, not only today, and on the weather service's estimate for that exact spot, which can differ from what you see locally. If the rain has really stopped, the alert closes by itself.

faqs.q: How does an alert close?
faqs.a: Automatically, once the rainfall has stayed below the danger level for two days in a row. The Status column then shows 'Resolved' and how it was closed. It is deliberately cautious: if the data is missing or old, the alert stays open.

faqs.q: What does 'Rain worsened' on an alert mean?
faqs.a: An alert is raised once and stays active while the rain keeps crossing its danger level. If the recent rain later gets clearly heavier — at least half a danger level higher than when the alert was last raised or updated — the alert is updated: it shows 'Rain worsened … ago' with how far above the danger level the rain is now, moves to the top of the list, shows as unread again in the bell, and the zone's subscribers get an update SMS. This is checked every hour and at most once every 6 hours per alert. The alert's own sentence does not change. Alerts that already existed before this feature start being measured at their next refresh and send nothing at first.

faqs.q: Which states raise rain alerts, and how?
faqs.a: Rain alerts use two rules. Sikkim uses its own published landslide study. Every other state uses the India Meteorological Department's national 'heavy rain' level: 64.5 mm in a day (51.6 mm on a high-risk road). That is a rainfall category, not a landslide-specific threshold. Alerts are raised only in states the team has switched on; where they are off, the page says 'Alerting not enabled' instead of showing 0, so a blank is not mistaken for safety.

faqs.q: What does the 'Broadcast' button on an alert row do?
faqs.a: It lets you push out a warning yourself: write your own headline and message, choose a severity (Moderate, High or Critical) and pick channels (SMS, app push, community sirens, the government CAP gateway). You must be signed in as an officer. Only SMS and the Critical phone calls are real today; the other channels are simulated and marked that way.

faqs.q: What does marking a broadcast 'Critical' do differently?
faqs.a: A Critical broadcast also places a real phone call to every official on the Authority Contacts page, reading your message aloud twice. Reserve Critical for situations that genuinely need someone's phone to ring — if every alert rang a phone, officials would start ignoring calls.

faqs.q: Where do citizen reports come from?
faqs.a: Residents submit them from the public reporting app on their phone, with a photo and a note. They arrive on the Citizen Reports page, marked 'Pending verification'. You must be signed in as an officer to see them.

faqs.q: How do I verify a report?
faqs.a: Click the report to open it. You get the photo, the exact location, the landmark, the time it was sent and the reporter's details. Once you have checked the site — in person or against the risk map — press 'Verify report' at the bottom right. The report is then marked Verified for everyone.

faqs.q: What does 'Verified' actually mean?
faqs.a: That an officer has confirmed the report describes something real. It does not mean the danger has been dealt with, and it does not create an incident record. Verification is not undone from this screen — contact the technical team if a mistake was made.

faqs.q: A report looks like a false alarm or a prank. What do I do?
faqs.a: Leave it as Pending and do not verify it. Repeated false reports from one number should be raised with the team who run the reporting app.

faqs.q: Is the reporter's phone number confidential?
faqs.a: It is visible only to signed-in officers, so you can call back for details. It is never shown publicly. Treat the number as official information and do not share it outside your office.

faqs.q: What is on the Incidents page?
faqs.a: Real past landslides recorded by the Geological Survey of India, for the state chosen at the top: the place and road section, the district, whether the slide is still active, and its coordinates. Use the filters and search to narrow them, and 'Check risk here' to see the risk around one. The survey does not record a date or a severity, so none is shown. All eight states are loaded (8,236 records in total); each state's own count is shown on its page.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an Alert and an Incident?
faqs.a: An alert is a warning raised when rain reaches a dangerous level for a road stretch. An incident, on the Incidents page, is a past landslide recorded by the Geological Survey of India. Not every alert becomes an incident. New landslides reported by residents are on the Citizen Reports page, where an officer can verify them.

faqs.q: The numbers have not changed all day. Is the system stuck?
faqs.a: Refresh the browser and check 'Rainfall updated … ago' beside the rainfall chart. Rainfall is refreshed about every hour. If it says many hours or days, tell the technical team — the hourly job may have stopped.

faqs.q: Which parts of this dashboard are real, and which are sample?
faqs.a: Real: risk zones and scores (from the model), rainfall (Open-Meteo, hourly), rain alerts for Sikkim and Assam (also shown in the scrolling strip at the top and in the notification bell), citizen reports, the landslide records on the Incidents page (all eight states), the Data & Observations status, and SMS and phone calls (trial account). Sample for now: only the profile panel. IMD's district rain warnings appear only as a snapshot fetched by hand; nothing from IMD updates automatically.

faqs.q: What does the Data & Observations page tell me?
faqs.a: It lists what the system is connected to, read from the running server: whether rainfall was updated recently, how many landslide records are loaded, and whether the SMS, AI-summary and photo services have credentials set. 'Connected' means set up, not tested at this moment, so 'Rainfall updated … ago' on the Overview is still the best freshness check.

faqs.q: 'System Health' shows less than 100%. What does that mean?
faqs.a: It shows whether the backend server is answering. Below 100% means it did not answer in time. Wait a minute and refresh — the free server can take up to a minute to wake up after being idle.

faqs.q: The map area is blank or grey.
faqs.a: The map background is loaded from the internet. A blank map usually means this computer has lost its connection, or a firewall is blocking it. The risk circles and all other data still work.

faqs.q: Who do I contact when something is genuinely broken?
faqs.a: Your state disaster management authority's technical contact. Tell them which page you were on, what you expected, what you saw, and the time — that is usually enough to diagnose it.

faqs.q: How do I sign in as an officer?
faqs.a: Click the lock icon at the top of the screen and enter the officer key given to you by your state's technical team. The key stays in this browser tab only and is forgotten when you close it.

faqs.q: What can I do without signing in?
faqs.a: Everyone can see the map, alerts, rainfall and 'Check my area'. Signing in is needed for actions and personal details: verifying citizen reports, reading reporters' phone numbers, sending broadcasts, managing Authority Contacts and updating risk scores.

faqs.q: Someone else needs access. How do they get it?
faqs.a: The officer key is issued by the technical team, not from inside this dashboard. Do not share it in chats or messages. If it may have been seen by others, ask the technical team to change it.

methodology.title: Data Sources & Methodology
methodology.subtitle: Every data source, model and AI feature this system uses — real, cited or simulated
methodology.whyBody: A system that decides when to warn people about a landslide should be able to say, plainly, where every number in it comes from. This page lists each data source, model and AI feature the dashboard relies on, labelled honestly: genuinely live, a real citation not yet independently confirmed, a rule the team designed itself, a real source that is switched off, or a feature that is not wired to a real gateway yet.

status.unverified: Real — cited source not independently verified
status.manual: Real — pushed by hand, not automatic

methodology.footer: This page is maintained by hand alongside the engineering docs (README.md) — if a source's status changes there, it should change here too. Access: the map, alerts, rainfall and 'Check my area' are public by design. Actions and personal data (verifying reports, reporters' phone numbers, broadcasts, contacts, updating risk scores) need an officer key — one shared key, not personal accounts.

items.name: Copernicus GLO-30 DEM
items.detail: 30 m global elevation model from AWS Open Data (no API key). Reprojected to a metre-based map projection before slope, aspect and curvature are worked out — without that step, slope comes out about 90° everywhere.

items.name: OpenStreetMap road network
items.detail: Each state's road geometry via the Overpass API, cut into corridor segments of about 500 m. Each segment is one prediction unit, so the map covers road corridors, not the whole state. Today: 104,145 segments across 7 states (Tripura is not loaded yet).

items.name: ESA WorldCover land cover
items.detail: 10 m resolution, 2021 v200 — the dominant land-cover class is taken for each corridor segment.

items.name: Landslide inventories (Geological Survey of India–linked)
items.detail: Real historical landslide points — the ground truth the models learn from. Sikkim: 765 verified points (777 raw records; 3 duplicate-coordinate points resolved). Each other state uses its own real inventory; see that state's training report. The records are also shown on the Incidents page — loaded for all eight states (8,236 records).

items.name: OpenStreetMap Nominatim place search
items.detail: Turns a typed village or town name into coordinates for 'Check my area'. A public service, restricted to the north-east and called only when Search is pressed.

items.name: OpenStreetMap villages and emergency services
items.detail: Named villages and towns, and hospitals, clinics, police and fire stations, downloaded from OpenStreetMap as a dated snapshot, stored in our database and shown around each road stretch. Volunteers map OpenStreetMap, so it is incomplete and can be out of date; distances are straight-line; coverage depends on what has been loaded (the download date is shown on the page). It does not say which villages would be cut off, and no rescue time is estimated.

items.name: Open-Meteo
items.detail: Daily rainfall: the past 20 days plus a 3-day forecast. A GitHub Actions job fetches it every hour for the highest-risk zones and stores it; for any other place it is fetched live in the browser when you look. It is the only rainfall source actually wired up.

items.name: IMD (India Meteorological Department)
items.detail: IMD has granted access to its API portal, and the dashboard can show a snapshot of its district rain warnings for the next 5 days, fetched by hand from one laptop before a demo. The key works only from one fixed IP address, which this system's hosting does not have, so nothing updates automatically. Open-Meteo feeds the rainfall data and this system's own alerts, not IMD.

items.name: Rainfall intensity-duration threshold (Sikkim)
items.detail: Harilal, Madhu, Ramesh & Pullarkatt (2019), Landslides 16(12), DOI 10.1007/s10346-019-01244-1 — a real, Sikkim-specific paper. It is paywalled, so its coefficients have not yet been independently confirmed against the primary text. Sikkim is the only state where rain alerts are switched on.

items.name: Rainfall threshold (Assam)
items.detail: From a real Guwahati study (Bhusan et al., 2014), with the coefficient re-derived and checked against the paper. It describes one city, not all of Assam, and it sits below ordinary monsoon rain (all 25 of Assam's highest-risk zones were over it in a normal monsoon month), so it is not used to alert. Assam uses the IMD baseline below.

items.name: Rainfall baseline for states without their own threshold (IMD heavy rain)
items.detail: The India Meteorological Department's 'heavy rain' level: 64.5 mm or more in 24 hours. It is a rainfall category IMD uses for its own warnings, not a landslide-specific threshold, so it is a baseline for a state with no published landslide threshold of its own, not a claim about exactly when slides start. One 24-hour window only; the team's susceptibility rule lowers it by 20% for high-risk roads. Confirmed from published summaries, not from IMD's own page.

items.name: Susceptibility × rainfall multiplier table
items.detail: Lowers the rainfall threshold for zones with a higher risk level. This weighting is the team's own explainable rule, not taken from a paper — said plainly here rather than dressed up as literature or as machine learning.

items.name: Alert auto-close rule
items.detail: An active alert closes by itself once rainfall has stayed below its danger level, in every duration window, for two days in a row. It is deliberately cautious: missing or old data keeps the alert open. This rule is the team's own.

items.name: Rain-worsened update rule
items.detail: An active alert is updated, and the zone's subscribers re-texted, when the recent rain (windows up to 5 days) is at least half a danger level higher than when the alert was last raised or updated — at most once every 6 hours per alert, and forecast days never count. The half-level step, the 6-hour gap and the 5-day limit are the team's own choices, not taken from a paper.

items.name: Per-state susceptibility models — Random Forest
items.detail: One Random Forest per state (Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram), trained on that state's real landslide points plus sampled non-landslide points and checked with spatially-buffered block cross-validation, not a naive random split. Reported ROC-AUC: Assam 0.95, Meghalaya 0.86, Manipur 0.82, Mizoram 0.71 (the weakest); the other states' figures are in their training reports. Risk levels are relative within each state.

items.name: Sikkim susceptibility model — Person B's Random Forest
items.detail: A separate, independently built pipeline (real DEM, real inventory, a RUSLE erosion model) — held-out AUC 0.774–0.782 on a plain 75/25 split, not the spatially-buffered check the other models use, which matters if they are compared side by side. Scores 3,411 of Sikkim's 3,921 zones.

items.name: Sikkim susceptibility model — Random Forest (extended features)
items.detail: Trained on 774 positive and 774 negative points, checked with 5-fold spatially-buffered block cross-validation. ROC-AUC 0.735. Scores the remaining 510 Sikkim zones — mostly one corridor (NH717A) that extends past the other model's raster coverage.

items.name: Citizen report triage summary
items.detail: A one-line summary of each citizen report for officers, always in English. Shown labelled "AI-generated triage summary" — never presented as the citizen's own words.

items.name: Alert bulletin draft ("Draft with AI")
items.detail: Proposes a headline and message from a zone's real rainfall and risk data in the Broadcast composer. Always reviewable and editable before sending — never sent automatically.

items.name: Citizen wording assist ("Clean up wording")
items.detail: Cleans up grammar and clarity in the citizen's own description before it is submitted — strictly forbidden from adding new facts (temperature 0.1). The citizen chooses "Use this" or keeps their own wording; nothing is applied automatically.

items.name: Citizen report translation
items.detail: Every report's description is translated to English for the dashboard and shown alongside — not instead of — the citizen's original wording.

items.name: Twilio SMS & voice
items.detail: Real dispatch — a critical broadcast has placed an actual phone call, confirmed by the recipient. It runs on a trial account, so only phone numbers manually verified in the Twilio console currently receive anything.

items.name: WhatsApp-ready alert copy
items.detail: No WhatsApp Business API is integrated. The Broadcast composer instead formats a paste-ready message that an officer copies into a real WhatsApp broadcast list by hand — honest about being a manual step, not an automatic send.

items.name: Mobile app push / community sirens / govt CAP XML gateway
items.detail: Selectable as broadcast channels and logged to the database as a real record, but no push, siren or CAP gateway is actually wired up yet — the confirmation banner says so explicitly at send time.

items.name: Supabase (Postgres + PostGIS, Storage)
items.detail: The live database and the storage for citizen-report photos. Photo URLs returned by the API are real, directly viewable Supabase Storage links.

items.name: Render (FastAPI hosting)
items.detail: The backend API is deployed here through a Blueprint (render.yaml), not run only on a laptop. On the free tier it sleeps when idle, so the first request can take up to a minute.

items.name: GitHub Actions (hourly rainfall job)
items.detail: Every hour a runner fetches rainfall from Open-Meteo and sends it to the backend, which stores it and raises or closes alerts. It runs outside the backend because Open-Meteo refuses requests from the backend host's shared address, and because the free backend sleeps when idle.
